Uncertainty remains in the track of a coastal system this weekend and what, if any, impacts it will have on our area.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
725 AM EDT Wed Sep 23 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 227 AM EDT Wednesday...

No significant changes were made to the forecast.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 227 AM EDT Wednesday...

1. Dry weather with seasonable temperatures will continue 
through Friday, with areas of frost likely again tonight. 

2. Uncertainty remains in the track of a coastal system this 
weekend and what, if any, impacts it will have on our area.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 227 AM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Broad high pressure remains firmly in place across 
southern Quebec/Ontario, spreading over the international border and 
into northern New York/New England. This feature shows no sign of 
budging over the next few days, and confidence has increased that we 
now will stay dry through at least Friday. Mostly clear skies will 
persist through Thursday, along with light winds. Temperatures will 
remain seasonable, with highs mainly in the 60s and lows in the 30s 
to near 40F. There will be another round of frost away from Lake 
Champlain tonight, and expect subsequent shifts will issue another 
Frost Advisory for tonight. 

Clouds start to increase Thursday night and Friday as low pressure 
off the Mid Atlantic coast attempts to force its way north toward 
coastal New England. Model guidance has come into better agreement 
in keeping any precipitation associated with this system shunted to 
our south through Friday, so no rain is expected in spite of the 
increasing cloud cover. Thursday will be a little warmer than the 
previous couple of days, with highs in the mid 60s to around 70F.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Models continue to exhibit differing solutions in how a 
coastal system will evolve as it meanders off the New England coast 
this weekend. Just how close to the coast it tracks is still 
uncertain, as is how far north and west its precipitation spreads 
inland. Given the strength of the high to our north and the extent 
of the dry air, it seems likely there will be a tight precipitation 
gradient on the northern/western side of the system, so small 
changes in track could result in significant changes in rain chances 
and amounts. There will also be a tightening pressure gradient over 
our area between the strengthening low and the high pressure 
anchored over southern Canada, so at the least expect winds to 
increase late this week and over the weekend, particularly over the 
higher terrain and down the Champlain Valley, where gusts of 25 to 
35 mph look possible, likely higher at summit level. 

One other potential impact from this system will be its effect on 
temperatures. With the very dry air currently in place, any rain 
that does hold together long enough to wrap back into our region 
would likely result in sharply cooler conditions; note that 
deterministic guidance lowers temperatures into the 50s where rain 
would be falling.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 12Z Thursday...Outside of patchy valley fog, VFR conditions
will prevail through the entire TAF period with skies remaining
SKC. Early morning fog will bring periods of IFR/LIFR 
conditions early in the TAF period, and then again after 07z Thu,
particularly at SLK/MPV/EFK. VCFG is also likely at BTV as 
river fog drifts over portions of the airfield. N/NE winds less
than 10 kt through the period, except SE at RUT. 

Outlook...

Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Friday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Friday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Saturday: VFR. Chance SHRA.
Saturday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Slight
chance SHRA.
Sunday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Chance SHRA.
